meta.engine: PostgreSQL 17.4 (private cluster, port 5439) + pgvector 0.8.0 HNSW (compiled from the v0.8.0 release tarball with MSVC 19.43; installed by running the extension SQL with MODULE_PATHNAME rewritten to the built vector.dll, because CREATE EXTENSION needs admin access to share/extension)
meta.pg_version: PostgreSQL 17.4 on x86_64-windows, compiled by msvc-19.42.34436, 64-bit

protocol.distance_operator: <-> (L2).  NOTE: pgvector maps <-> to L2 and <=> to cosine; using <=> against a vector_l2_ops index is silently seq-scanned (no error).  All searches here use <->.
protocol.data: xb = default_rng(seed).random((20000,64), float32); qb = same stream, (200,64); exact top-10 by numpy
protocol.episode: search1 -> engine structural rewrite (CLUSTER and/or REINDEX) -> search2; table content unchanged, so any top-10 difference is an index-generation tear (A4)

sql_used.create_table: CREATE TABLE g_vectors (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, embedding vector(64))
sql_used.clean_generation_A: CREATE TABLE g_vectors (...); INSERT 20000 rows in id order; CREATE INDEX g_vectors_embedding_hnsw ON g_vectors USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops) WITH (m=32, ef_construction=64)   -- built BEFORE the perm column exists (clean; no dead-tuple pollution)
sql_used.legacy_generation_A: the original cell_g order: build the HNSW index first, THEN ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN perm int + UPDATE (non-HOT -> 20k dead index entries), THEN search
sql_used.search: SELECT id FROM g_vectors ORDER BY embedding <-> $$[..]$$::vector LIMIT 10   (SET hnsw.ef_search=64)
sql_used.generation_change_A_to_B: CLUSTER g_vectors USING g_vectors_perm_idx;  REINDEX INDEX g_vectors_embedding_hnsw
sql_used.permutation: ALTER TABLE g_vectors ADD COLUMN perm int; SELECT setseed(<frac>); UPDATE g_vectors AS t SET perm = s.r FROM (SELECT id, (row_number() OVER (ORDER BY random()))::int AS r FROM g_vectors) s WHERE t.id = s.id; CREATE INDEX g_vectors_perm_idx ON g_vectors (perm)
sql_used.reindex_with_efc: ALTER INDEX g_vectors_embedding_hnsw SET (ef_construction = <efc>); REINDEX INDEX g_vectors_embedding_hnsw
sql_used.pinned_read: SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; <search1>; [second connection: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY]; <search2>; COMMIT
sql_used.baseline_approx: same generation, SET hnsw.ef_search in {16,32,64,128}, pairwise set disagreement
sql_used.session_setup: SET dynamic_library_path = '<pgvector build dir>;$libdir'  (so parallel maintenance workers can dlopen vector.dll)

meta.headline_finding: The paper's G tear (legacy protocol, 0.895 on seed 20261008) does NOT survive recall matching.  Root cause, measured: the legacy generation A was the HNSW index searched AFTER a non-HOT UPDATE that wrote the permutation; that UPDATE left 20 000 dead index entries (n_tup_hot_upd = 0), which halves A's recall (~0.94 -> ~0.76) and inflates the A-vs-B tear.  Building A cleanly (before the UPDATE) makes both generations' recall agree (~0.94) and the tear drops accordingly.  The residual clean tear is reported per seed and compared against the same-generation approximation baseline.
deviations: pgvector 0.8.0 was recompiled from the release tarball (MSVC 19.43) and installed by running the extension SQL with MODULE_PATHNAME rewritten to the built vector.dll (no admin write to share/extension).  Because vector.dll is outside $libdir, parallel maintenance workers could not dlopen it (error: could not access file "vector"); every session sets dynamic_library_path to the build dir so parallel index builds work.

CONFOUND FOUND AND REMOVED: the original cell_g searched generation A only AFTER a non-HOT UPDATE wrote the permutation; that left 20 000 dead HNSW index entries (pg_stat n_tup_upd=20000, n_tup_hot_upd=0), dropping A's recall from ~0.94 to ~0.76 and inflating the tear.  The clean protocol builds generation A before the UPDATE; the legacy (polluted) variant is still measured and reported for transparency.
A first run of this script was aborted and re-run after the confound above was diagnosed; only the clean run's cells are stored here.
limitations: pgvector exposes no HNSW adjacency; only the answer-level (A4) any-difference convention is measurable in-engine (see cell CONV).

the permutation for CLUSTER is generated server-side with setseed()+random() (a client-side 20k-row UPDATE was ~100x slower); it is reproducible per setseed value but is not the numpy rng the FAISS protocol uses.
ef_construction >= 2*m is enforced by pgvector; the sweep uses {64,96,128,192,256} (>=64).

the CLUSTER/REINDEX rebuild is not bit-reproducible (cell DET of the original run: ~4.5-7% of episodes change between two consecutive rebuilds of the SAME heap order, by <=2 ids).  That is the floor under every generation-vs-generation number.

measured_predicate.paper_structural_tear_convention: |res_A delta res_B| > max(noise_A, noise_B)  -- requires the index adjacency and a per-index noise level
measured_predicate.which_one_is_used_here: any-difference (set inequality); every cell's per_episode block stores {set_equal, ordered_equal, symdiff} so both readings are recoverable

CONV.adjacency_export_question: does pgvector expose the HNSW adjacency of a built index?

probes.pg_version: PostgreSQL 17.4 on x86_64-windows, compiled by msvc-19.42.34436, 64-bit
explain_sample: ->  Index Scan using g_vectors_embedding_hnsw on g_vectors

CONV.conclusion: pgvector's HNSW index is a CUSTOM access method whose pages are opaque to SQL: it appears in pg_index/pg_class as a normal index relation but exposes NO relation, view, function or GUC returning a node's adjacency/neighbour list (pg_proc has no hnsw/neighbour accessor; pg_indexes surfaces only name/tablespace/indexdef; EXPLAIN prints only 'Index Scan using ... hnsw').  Therefore the paper's structural-tear convention |res_A delta res_B| > max(noise_A, noise_B) CANNOT be evaluated inside pgvector; only the answer-level any-difference convention is measurable in-engine.  (FAISS, by contrast, exposes index.hnsw.neighbors / .offsets.)
